## Warm-Up: Quick Concept and Calculation Checks

a. A town's population grows from 8,000 to 8,400 in one year. What is the population growth rate?
b. A country's real GDP is $50 million and its population is 25,000. What is real GDP per capita?
c. A household saves $500 per month. How much total saving does that household contribute in one
   year?
d. A $10,000 investment is expected to generate $800 per year in profit. What is the expected
   rate of return?
e. A retiree buys 10 shares of an existing company's stock on the stock market. Does this count as
   *Investment* in the economic sense? Why or why not?
f. A bakery purchases a new industrial oven to expand production. Does this count as *Investment*
   in the economic sense? Why or why not?
g. A landlord signs a 12-month apartment lease with tenants at a fixed monthly rent. Is this price
   sticky or flexible?
h. The price of Bitcoin on a cryptocurrency exchange. Is this price sticky or flexible?

<!-- <details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

a. $(8{,}400 - 8{,}000)/8{,}000 = 5$ percent.
b. $\$50{,}000{,}000 / 25{,}000 = \$2{,}000$ per person.
c. $\$500 \times 12 = \$6{,}000$ per year.
d. $\$800 / \$10{,}000 = 8$ percent.
e. *No.* Buying existing shares just transfers ownership of an already-existing asset from one
   person to another, it does not create any new capital.
f. *Yes.* A new oven is new capital equipment that expands the firm's ability to produce, exactly
   what economic Investment means.
g. *Sticky.* The rent is locked in by a 12-month lease regardless of changing market conditions.
h. *Flexible.* Cryptocurrency prices trade continuously on an exchange and adjust to new
   information almost instantly.

</details> -->

## Problem 1: Total Growth vs. Per-Capita Growth

A country's real GDP grows from $18.0 trillion to $18.9 trillion over one year. Over that same
year, the country's population grows from 300 million to 306 million people.

a. What is the percentage growth rate of total real GDP?
b. What is real GDP per capita in each year?
c. What is the percentage growth rate of real GDP per capita?
d. Why is the answer to (c) smaller than the answer to (a)?

<!-- <details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

a. Growth rate of total real GDP = ($18.9 trillion minus $18.0 trillion) divided by $18.0 trillion
   = $0.9 trillion divided by $18.0 trillion = *5.0 percent*.
b. Real GDP per capita, year 1: $18.0 trillion divided by 300 million = *$60,000*. Year 2: $18.9
   trillion divided by 306 million = *$61,765* (rounded).
c. Growth rate of real GDP per capita = ($61,765 minus $60,000) divided by $60,000 = *about 2.9
   percent*.
d. Total output grew 5.0 percent, but population also grew (from 300 million to 306 million, a 2.0
   percent increase). Since that larger output has to be divided among more people, the *increase
   in living standards per person* is smaller than the increase in total output. This is why
   economists track GDP *per capita*, not just total GDP, when asking whether people are actually
   getting better off.

</details> -->

## Problem 2: Saving, Investment, and Expected Returns

A firm is deciding whether to build a new factory that costs $5 million. The firm forecasts the
factory would generate $600,000 in additional profit per year.

a. What annual rate of return does the firm expect on this $5 million investment?
b. If interest rates rise and the firm could instead earn a guaranteed 8 percent per year by simply
   depositing that $5 million in a bank, should the firm still build the factory? Explain using the
   idea of expected returns.
c. Explain, in one or two sentences, why a general rise in interest rates throughout the economy
   tends to reduce the total amount of economic investment.

<!-- <details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

a. Expected rate of return = $600,000 divided by $5,000,000 = *12 percent* per year.
b. The factory still expected to return 12 percent, comfortably more than the *guaranteed* 8
   percent from a bank deposit, so the firm should still build it. The factory return does carry
   more risk than a bank deposit, but as long as the firm believes 12 percent is the fair expected
   return for that risk, it remains the better choice.
c. Investment projects only get funded when the expected return on the project beats the return
   available elsewhere, such as a bank deposit or bond. When interest rates rise economy-wide, the
   bar an investment project has to clear rises too, so *fewer* projects have an expected return
   high enough to be worth funding, and total investment falls.

</details> -->

## Problem 3: When the Average Isn't the Typical Household

A small country has exactly 5 households. Their annual incomes in Year 1 and Year 2 are:

| Household | Year 1 Income | Year 2 Income |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $30,000 | $31,000 |
| 2 | $32,000 | $33,000 |
| 3 | $35,000 | $36,000 |
| 4 | $38,000 | $39,000 |
| 5 | $65,000 | $111,000 |

a. Compute the mean (average) household income in Year 1 and in Year 2, and the growth rate of
   the mean.
b. Compute the median household income in Year 1 and in Year 2 (the income of the middle
   household when incomes are sorted low to high), and the growth rate of the median.
c. A news report says "average income in this country grew 25 percent this year." Is that
   statement misleading? Why or why not?
d. Relate this example back to the GDP per capita versus median household income discussion from
   the slides. Why might a country with healthy GDP-per-capita growth still have a lot of
   unhappy citizens?

<!-- <details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center

import plotly.graph_objects as go

BLUE = "#1f4e79"
ORANGE = "#c55a11"

households = ["HH 1", "HH 2", "HH 3", "HH 4", "HH 5"]
year1 = [30000, 32000, 35000, 38000, 65000]
year2 = [31000, 33000, 36000, 39000, 111000]

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=households, y=year1, name="Year 1", marker_color=BLUE))
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=households, y=year2, name="Year 2", marker_color=ORANGE))
fig.add_hline(y=40000, line_dash="dash", line_color=BLUE,
              annotation_text="Year 1 mean: $40,000", annotation_position="top left")
fig.add_hline(y=50000, line_dash="dash", line_color=ORANGE,
              annotation_text="Year 2 mean: $50,000", annotation_position="top right")

fig.update_layout(
    barmode="group", yaxis_title="Household income",
    width=640, height=420, plot_bgcolor="white",
    legend=dict(x=0.4, y=1.15, orientation="h")
)
fig.update_yaxes(showgrid=True, gridwidth=1, gridcolor="lightgray", tickformat="$,.0f")
fig.show()
```

a. Mean, Year 1: $(30{,}000+32{,}000+35{,}000+38{,}000+65{,}000)/5 = 200{,}000/5 = \$40{,}000$.
   Mean, Year 2: $(31{,}000+33{,}000+36{,}000+39{,}000+111{,}000)/5 = 250{,}000/5 = \$50{,}000$.
   Growth rate of the mean: $(50{,}000-40{,}000)/40{,}000 = 25$ percent.
b. Median, Year 1 (middle of 30, 32, 35, 38, 65): *$35,000*.
   Median, Year 2 (middle of 31, 33, 36, 39, 111): *$36,000*.
   Growth rate of the median: $(36{,}000-35{,}000)/35{,}000 \approx 2.9$ percent.
c. It is *technically true but misleading*. The 25 percent figure is entirely driven by Household
   5, whose income nearly doubled, while the other four households, four out of five people in
   this economy, saw incomes rise only about 3 percent. The "average person" implied by the mean
   does not resemble any actual household here.
d. GDP per capita is a mean, just like average income in this example. When growth is
   concentrated among a relatively small share of the population, GDP per capita can rise
   substantially even while the typical (median) household's living standard barely improves. That
   gap between a healthy aggregate statistic and a stagnant typical experience is exactly the kind
   of thing that can make official "the economy is growing" headlines feel disconnected from how
   most people actually feel.

</details> -->

## Problem 4: The Market for Loanable Funds

Chapter 3 introduced supply and demand for goods, like soybeans or textbooks. The same model can
describe the market where saving meets investment, called the **market for loanable funds**.
*Savers* supply funds to this market (depositing money in banks, buying bonds), hoping to earn
interest. *Borrowers*, often firms that want to invest, demand funds from this market, and have to
pay interest to get them.

The table below shows the (hypothetical) market for loanable funds in a country.

| Interest Rate | Quantity of Saving Supplied | Quantity of Investment Demanded |
|---|---|---|
| 2% | $100 billion | $400 billion |
| 3% | $150 billion | $350 billion |
| 4% | $200 billion | $300 billion |
| 5% | $250 billion | $250 billion |
| 6% | $300 billion | $200 billion |
| 7% | $350 billion | $150 billion |

a. Why does it make sense to treat saving as a *supply* curve and investment as
   a *demand* curve in this market? What plays the role of "price"?
b. Using the table, what is the equilibrium interest rate, and what quantity of funds gets loaned
   at that rate?
c. Suppose the interest rate is temporarily stuck at 3 percent. Is there a shortage or surplus of
   loanable funds at that rate, and how large? Which direction would you expect the interest rate
   to move to restore equilibrium?
d. Using what you learned about supply and demand shifts in Chapter 3: if a new government policy
   encourages people to save more at every interest rate (the saving curve shifts right), what
   happens to the equilibrium interest rate and the equilibrium quantity of loanable funds?
<!-- 
<details>
<summary>Show Answer</summary>

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center

import plotly.graph_objects as go

BLUE = "#1f4e79"
ORANGE = "#c55a11"

rate = [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]
saving = [100, 150, 200, 250, 300, 350]
investment = [400, 350, 300, 250, 200, 150]

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=saving, y=rate, mode="lines", name="Saving (supply of funds)",
    line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3),
    hovertemplate="Interest rate: %{y}%<br>Quantity: $%{x}B<extra></extra>"
))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=investment, y=rate, mode="lines", name="Investment (demand for funds)",
    line=dict(color=ORANGE, width=3),
    hovertemplate="Interest rate: %{y}%<br>Quantity: $%{x}B<extra></extra>"
))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=[250], y=[5], mode="markers+text", text=["Equilibrium"], textposition="bottom right",
    marker=dict(size=11, color="black"), showlegend=False,
    hovertemplate="Equilibrium<br>Interest rate: 5%<br>Quantity: $250B<extra></extra>"
))

fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title="Quantity of loanable funds ($ billions)", yaxis_title="Interest rate",
    width=560, height=420, plot_bgcolor="white",
    legend=dict(x=0.35, y=1.18, orientation="h", font=dict(size=10))
)
fig.update_xaxes(showgrid=True, gridwidth=1, gridcolor="lightgray")
fig.update_yaxes(showgrid=True, gridwidth=1, gridcolor="lightgray", ticksuffix="%")
fig.show()
```

a. Savers act like sellers, they supply more funds to the market as the reward for doing so (the
   interest rate) rises, just like a seller offers more of a good as its price rises. Borrowers act
   like buyers, they demand fewer funds as the cost of borrowing (the interest rate) rises, just
   like a buyer demands less of a good as its price rises. The *interest rate* plays the role of
   price in this market.
b. Equilibrium interest rate is *5 percent*, where quantity of saving supplied equals quantity of
   investment demanded, both equal *$250 billion*.
c. At 3 percent, quantity of saving supplied is $150 billion but quantity of investment demanded is
   $350 billion. That is a *shortage* of loanable funds of *$200 billion*, borrowers want far more
   funds than savers are offering at that low rate. Just like a shortage in a goods market, this
   pushes the interest rate *up* toward the $5$ percent equilibrium, as borrowers compete for the
   scarce funds available.
d. This is exactly the same logic as a rightward supply shift in Chapter 3: more funds supplied at
   every interest rate pushes the equilibrium interest rate *down* and the equilibrium quantity of
   loanable funds *up*. Cheaper borrowing (a lower interest rate) is also exactly the kind of change
   that, from the investment decisions slide, would encourage firms to invest more.

</details> -->
